#1
L: This imperishable yoga to-Vivasvat I-declared; Vivasvat to-Manu told [it]; Manu to-Ikṣvāku said [it].
I: The Blessed Lord said: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat; Vivasvat told it to Manu; Manu told it to Ikṣvāku.
N: A chain of transmission opens the chapter: Vivasvat, the sun-god, to his son Manu (the first man and lawgiver), to Manu's son Ikṣvāku (first king of the solar dynasty, ancestor of Rāma). Proktavān, a perfect participle standing in for a finite verb ('I have declared, taught'), is a common Epic construction for the first person perfect. The claim of vast antiquity here sets up Arjuna's puzzled objection in verse 4 and Kṛṣṇa's answer about his own repeated births in verse 5.
#2
L: Thus, through-succession-attained, this the-royal-sages knew; that, by-great time here, yoga lost [became], O scorcher-of-the-foe.
I: Handed down in this succession, the royal sages knew this yoga; but with the passing of great time it was lost here, scorcher of the foe.
N: Paramparā-prāptam, 'received through an unbroken succession', describes how the yoga in verse 1 continued to be known — by rājarṣayaḥ, 'royal sages' (kings who were also seers, like Ikṣvāku's line, and Janaka at 3.20). Kālena mahatā, 'through great time', explains why Kṛṣṇa must now teach it again: not a new doctrine, but a recovery of one that had lapsed.
#3
L: That very-same, by-me, to-you today, yoga [has been] declared, ancient — for devoted you-are to-me, [and my] friend; a-secret, indeed, this, supreme.
I: That very same ancient yoga I have now declared to you, because you are my devotee and my friend; for this is a supreme secret.
N: Sa eva ayam, 'that very same one', insists this is the identical ancient teaching of verses 1-2, not something newly invented for Arjuna's benefit. Bhakto 'si me sakhā ca, 'you are my devotee and my friend', gives the reason Arjuna specifically receives it: devotion and friendship together, not merit or birth. Rahasyam ... uttamam, 'a supreme secret', is neuter, referring to the teaching itself.
#4
L: Later [is] your birth; earlier, the-birth of-Vivasvat. How this might-I-understand: 'you at-the-beginning declared [it]' — thus [you say]?
I: Arjuna said: Your birth was later, and Vivasvat's birth was earlier. How am I to understand this — that you taught it at the very beginning?
N: Apara and para here mean 'later' and 'earlier' respectively, a temporal sense of para distinct from its more usual 'higher, supreme'; Śaṅkara glosses aparam as arvācīnam ('recent') and param as pūrvam ('prior'). Arjuna's objection is simple chronology: Kṛṣṇa, born in his own generation, could not literally have taught the sun-god at the dawn of the solar line — setting up the doctrine of verse 5.
#5
L: Many, of-mine, have-passed, births, and of-yours, O Arjuna; those I know all; not you know, O scorcher-of-the-foe.
I: The Blessed Lord said: Many births of mine have passed, Arjuna, and yours as well; I know them all, but you do not, scorcher of the foe.
N: Kṛṣṇa's answer to verse 4: rebirth is not in dispute — both he and Arjuna have had bahūni janmāni, 'many births' — the difference is that Kṛṣṇa vetti sarvāṇi, 'knows them all', while ordinary beings like Arjuna do not (na tvaṃ vettha). This unbroken divine memory, not a denial of prior existence, is what makes the claim of verse 1 possible, and it leads directly into verse 6's account of how such births occur at all.
#6
L: Unborn although, and imperishable-in-nature, of-beings the-lord although, being — my-own nature having-taken-control-of, I-come-to-be through-my-own-power-of-illusion.
I: Although I am unborn and imperishable in nature, and the lord of all beings, I come into being by taking control of my own nature, through my own creative power.
N: Two concessive clauses frame the paradox: ajaḥ api san, 'though being unborn', and bhūtānām īśvaraḥ api san, 'though being lord of beings' (with avyaya-ātmā, 'of imperishable nature', an added epithet). Against this, saṃbhavāmi, 'I come to be', is explained not as compulsion by karma (as ordinary beings are driven, 3.5) but as a deliberate act: svāṃ prakṛtim adhiṣṭhāya, 'having mastered his own nature', through ātma-māyā, 'his own creative power' — the doctrinal basis for the avatāra teaching of the next two verses.
#7
L: Whenever indeed of dharma a fading comes to be, O Bhārata, a rising-up of adharma — then I send forth myself.
I: Whenever dharma wanes, Bhārata, and its opposite rises, I bring myself forth.
N: Yadā yadā, 'whenever, whenever' (doubled for generality), answers to tadā, 'then', in the second line — the same relative-correlative pattern seen at 3.21-22. Dharmasya glāniḥ, 'a wasting of dharma', and adharmasya abhyutthānam, 'a rising-up of adharma', stand in exact parallel. This is the poem's classic statement of periodic divine descent, completed by verse 8's statement of its threefold purpose. House rendering used per convention.
#8
L: For the rescue of the good and for the destruction of evil-doers, for the purpose of establishing dharma, I come to be age after age.
I: To rescue the good, to destroy those who do evil, and to set dharma firmly in place, I am born in every age.
N: Three parallel datives of purpose — paritrāṇāya, vināśāya, dharma-saṃsthāpana-arthāya — govern the one verb sambhavāmi. Yuge yuge, 'age after age' (another doubled word, like yadā yadā in verse 7), completes the doctrine of verse 7 with its threefold aim: protecting the good, destroying evildoers, re-establishing dharma. Together 4.7-8 are among the Gītā's most quoted verses. House rendering used per convention.
#9
L: Birth and action, my, divine, thus who knows in-truth — having-given-up the-body, rebirth not attains; to-me he-attains, O Arjuna.
I: One who truly knows in this way my divine birth and action does not, on giving up the body, take birth again — he comes to me, Arjuna.
N: Janma and karma, both objects of vetti, are qualified as divyam, 'divine' — Kṛṣṇa's voluntary incarnation (verse 6) and its purpose (verses 7-8), not ordinary karma-driven birth and action. Knowing this tattvataḥ, 'as it truly is', is what frees one from punarjanma, 'rebirth', and grants mām eti, 'he comes to me' — the doctrine of union with Kṛṣṇa developed further in later chapters (8.5-7, 9.34, 18.65).
#10
L: Free-from-passion-fear-and-anger, absorbed-in-me, in-me taken-refuge — many, through-the-austerity-of-knowledge purified, to-my-state-of-being have-come.
I: Many, free from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, purified by the discipline of knowledge, have attained my very being.
N: The promise of verse 9 is generalized to bahavaḥ, 'many' seekers across time. Vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhāḥ, 'free from passion, fear and anger', names the threefold freedom required; jñāna-tapasā pūtāḥ, 'purified by the austerity of knowledge', names the means, recalling jñāna-yoga at 3.3. Mad-bhāvam āgatāḥ, 'have come to my very being', intensifies verse 9's mām eti.
#11
L: Who as to-me they-approach, them so, indeed, I-favor; my path men follow, O Pārtha, in-every-way.
I: In whatever way people approach me, I reward them in that same way; men follow my path in every way, Pārtha.
N: A relative-correlative pair, ye ... yathā ... tān ... tathā (cf. yadā ... tadā, verse 7), states a striking reciprocity: bhajāmi, 'I favor, I share in return' (the root behind bhakti), meets each worshipper on the terms of their own approach. This much-debated verse is read by some as an early statement that all sincere paths, however conceived, ultimately lead to Kṛṣṇa.
#12
L: Desiring, of-actions the-fruit, they-worship here the-gods; quickly, indeed, in-the-human world, success comes-to-be, born-of-action.
I: Those who desire the fruits of action worship the gods in this world, for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
N: Yajante is the underlying form of yajanta before iha; the final -e shifts to -a before a following short vowel, the same rare sandhi already met at 3.28's vartanta. The verse candidly names a lesser motive — kāṅkṣantaḥ karmaṇāṃ siddhim, 'desiring the fruit of action' (precisely what 2.47's house rendering warns against) — driving ordinary worship of minor deities, because such results come kṣipram, 'quickly', in the human world; Śaṅkara treats this as a description of common practice, not the poem's own recommendation.
#13
L: The-fourfold-class-system by-me [was] created, according-to-the-division-of-guṇa-and-action; of-it the-doer, although, me, know [as] the-non-doer, imperishable.
I: I created the fourfold order of classes, according to the division of the guṇas and their actions; yet know me, though its author, to be the non-doer, and imperishable.
N: Cāturvarṇyam, 'the fourfold class-system' (the four varṇas, taken up again at 18.41-44), is traced to Kṛṣṇa's own creative act, but guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ, 'according to the division of guṇa and action' — each class corresponding to a distribution of the three guṇas and its characteristic work, applying chapter 3's guṇa-doctrine (3.27-29) to society itself. The second line then applies that same doctrine to Kṛṣṇa: tasya kartāram api mām ... akartāram avyayam, 'me, though its maker, know as the non-doer, unchanging' — paralleling verse 6's claim that his own action does not bind him.
#14
L: Not me actions stain; not for-me in-the-fruit-of-action [is-there] longing. Thus who me knows-fully — by-actions not he is-bound.
I: Actions do not stain me, nor do I long for the fruit of action. Whoever knows me in this way is not bound by actions.
N: A summary statement of what verses 6 and 13 have just claimed of Kṛṣṇa: na māṃ karmāṇi limpanti, 'actions do not stain me', and na me karma-phale spṛhā, 'I have no longing for the fruit of action' — the latter echoing the house rendering of 2.47 as Kṛṣṇa's own standing example of unattached action. Iti māṃ yo 'bhijānāti, 'whoever thus knows me', extends the same release from karmic bondage (karmabhir na sa badhyate) already promised in verse 9, now grounded in this understanding of Kṛṣṇa's nature, closing the chapter's opening movement before the extended teaching on action itself resumes.
#15
L: Thus having-known, action [was] done even-by-former seekers-of-liberation; do action, indeed, you, therefore — by-the-ancients, more-anciently, done.
I: Knowing this, even the sages of old who sought liberation performed action; therefore you too should act, just as it was done by the ancients, and by those before them still.
N: Kṛtaṃ karma pūrvaiḥ, 'action was done by the ancients' (the past participle kṛtam functioning almost as a finite verb, with the agent pūrvaiḥ in the instrumental, as with any passive participle), continues the argument of verses 9-14 into direct address: even mumukṣubhiḥ, 'those desiring liberation' (from muc, the poem's first use of this term), still acted. Pūrvaiḥ pūrvataraṃ kṛtam, 'done by the ancients, done still more anciently', doubles the appeal to precedent, much as ch. 3's Janaka argument (3.20) did.
#16
L: What [is] action? What [is] inaction? — thus even-the-wise, here, [are] confused. That to-you action I-will-declare, knowing which you-will-be-freed from-evil.
I: 'What is action? What is inaction?' Even the wise are confused about this. I will explain to you what action is, and knowing it you will be freed from evil.
N: Kavayaḥ, 'seers, sages' (kavi, MW's older sense of an inspired poet-seer, not merely 'poet'), admits that even they are mohitāḥ, 'confused', about the very distinction the chapter is about to draw — kiṃ karma kim akarma, 'what is action, what is inaction', posed as two nominal questions closed by iti. Aśubhāt, 'from evil, misfortune', names the reward of understanding it: mokṣyase, 'you will be released', from the same root as mumukṣu in verse 15.
#17
L: Of-action, indeed, even, [something] is-to-be-known, and is-to-be-known of-wrong-action; and of-inaction is-to-be-known — deep [is] the-course of-action.
I: One must understand what action is, and what wrong action is, and what inaction is as well — for the way of action is hard to fathom.
N: The verse names a third term beside karma and akarma: vikarma, 'wrong, forbidden action' — introduced here for the first time in the poem. Boddhavyam, 'is to be known', a gerundive used impersonally three times, states that all three must be understood before the paradox of the next verse can make sense; gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ, 'the course of action is deep [i.e. hard to fathom]', is Kṛṣṇa's own warning that what follows is subtle.
#18
L: Who inaction-in-action sees, and who action-in-inaction — he [is] wise among-men, he [is] disciplined, a-doer-of-all-action.
I: The one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among men; he is disciplined, and he has accomplished everything there is to do.
N: The chapter's most quoted paradox, built on the three terms just distinguished in verse 17: karmaṇy akarma ... akarmaṇi ca karma, 'inaction in action ... action in inaction', a chiastic double relative clause (yaḥ ... yaḥ) resolved only by identifying true action and inaction with attachment and its absence, not with outward movement or stillness — the same point ch. 3.4-7 made about the hypocrite who is outwardly still but inwardly active. Kṛtsna-karma-kṛt, 'one who has done all action', restates ch. 3.19's kāryaṃ karma in a single compound.
#19
L: Whose all undertakings [are] free-from-desire-and-intention — him, whose-action-is-burnt-by-the-fire-of-knowledge, they-call learned, the-wise.
I: The wise call him learned whose every undertaking is free of desire and intention, and whose actions have been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
N: Jñānāgni-dagdha-karmāṇam, 'whose action is burnt by the fire of knowledge', is the chapter's first use of the jñānāgni image, an image the poem returns to later in this chapter (v. 37, in the next batch); saṃkalpa, 'intention, deliberate resolve' (distinct from mere kāma, 'desire'), pairs with it to describe what such action lacks. Paṇḍitam, 'learned, wise', echoes 2.11's first use of the term for one who truly understands, rather than merely knows facts.
#20
L: Having-abandoned attachment-to-the-fruit-of-action, ever-content, without-support — though engaged in-action, not-at-all anything does he.
I: Having given up attachment to the fruit of his actions, ever content and dependent on nothing, he does nothing at all, even while he is engaged in action.
N: Karma-phala-āsaṅgam, 'attachment to the fruit of action', restates the house rendering of 2.47 in compound form. Karmaṇy abhipravṛttaḥ api naiva kiṃcit karoti, '[though] engaged in action, he does nothing at all', is a deliberate paradox like verse 18's: 'does nothing' means he incurs no fresh result, not that he is physically idle, as the next two verses go on to make concrete.
#21
L: Without-hope, restrained-in-mind-and-self, having-abandoned-all-possessions — mere bodily action doing, he-incurs-not sin.
I: Free of expectation, his mind and self restrained, having given up all possessions, doing only what the body requires, he incurs no fault.
N: Śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma, 'mere bodily action', names the minimal residue of activity even such a man still performs — bare bodily necessity, the same idea as ch. 3.8's śarīra-yātrā, 'the maintenance of the body' — without incurring kilbiṣam, 'sin, moral fault' (cf. 3.13). Nir-āśis, 'without hope [of gain]', and tyakta-sarva-parigrahaḥ, 'having renounced all possessions', sharpen verse 20's nirāśrayaḥ into concrete terms.
#22
L: Content-with-gain-that-comes-unsought, beyond-the-pairs-of-opposites, free-from-envy; equal in-success and-in-failure — even having-acted, he-is-not bound.
I: Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, free of envy, equal in success and failure — even when he acts, he is not bound.
N: Dvandva, 'a pair' (here of opposites such as pleasure and pain, heat and cold), is a technical term the poem develops further in later chapters (7.27-28, 15.5); samaḥ siddhāv asiddhau ca, 'equal in success and failure', restates in explicit terms the evenness of mind the house rendering of 2.47 already implied. Kṛtvā api na nibadhyate, 'even having acted, he is not bound', is the plainest statement yet of the chapter's central claim.
#23
L: Of-one-whose-attachment-is-gone, of-the-liberated, whose-mind-is-established-in-knowledge — acting for-the-sake-of-sacrifice, action, wholly, dissolves-away.
I: For one who is free of attachment, liberated, his mind fixed in knowledge, and who acts only for the sake of sacrifice — his action dissolves away completely.
N: Four descriptions of the same man (gata-saṅgasya, muktasya, jñāna-avasthita-cetasaḥ, ācarataḥ, all genitive) build up to a single claim about karma, the grammatical subject: samagraṃ pravilīyate, 'dissolves away entirely' — a stronger image than verses 20-22's 'not bound', reserved for one who, like ch. 3.9's yajñārthāt karma, acts specifically yajñāya, 'for sacrifice'. This closes the run of descriptions of the liberated actor (vv. 19-23) and turns the chapter, from verse 24, to sacrifice itself.
#24
L: Brahman [is] the-offering, brahman [is] the-oblation, into-the-brahman-fire, by-brahman, offered; brahman alone, by-him, [is] to-be-reached, whose-absorption-is-in-brahman-action.
I: The offering is brahman, the oblation is brahman, poured by brahman into the fire that is brahman; and brahman alone is what is reached by one whose action is wholly absorbed in brahman.
N: One of the poem's most famous sentences, built entirely on the word brahman (kept untranslated), repeated six times, each in a different grammatical role: nominative as the offering-vessel (arpaṇam) and again as the oblation (havis), locative as the fire it is poured into (brahmāgnau), instrumental as the one who pours it (brahmaṇā), nominative once more (with eva) as the goal reached, and finally instrumental in the closing compound brahma-karma-samādhinā, 'absorbed in brahman-action', describing the person who reaches it. The pattern states that every element of the sacrificial act — instrument, material, fire, agent and result — is nothing other than brahman; recognizing this, as verse 23 already said, dissolves the action away, and the one so absorbed reaches brahman itself. The teaching echoes ch. 3.15's brahmodbhavaṃ karma, which likewise traced karma back to brahman.
#25
L: The-divine sacrifice alone, some, yogins, attend-upon; others, into-the-brahman-fire, the-sacrifice, by-sacrifice-itself, offer-up.
I: Some yogins worship only through sacrifice offered to the gods; others offer sacrifice itself as an oblation into the fire that is brahman.
N: This opens the chapter's catalogue of the many things called yajña, 'sacrifice' (through verse 33, continuing into the next batch), starting with the plainest form — daivam yajñam, ritual offering to the gods — set against those who instead treat the very act of sacrifice as an oblation poured into the brahman-fire just described in verse 24. Juhvati and its compound upajuhvati, 'they offer, pour as oblation', are the verbs that will recur through verse 27.
#26
L: The-senses-beginning-with-hearing, others, into-the-fires-of-restraint, offer; the-objects-beginning-with-sound, others, into-the-fires-of-the-senses, offer.
I: Some offer the senses themselves, beginning with hearing, as oblations into the fires of restraint; others offer the objects of sense, beginning with sound, into the fires of the senses.
N: Śrotra-ādīni and śabda-ādīn both use ādi, 'beginning [with]', the standard way of naming an open list by its first member (as with avyaktādīni bhūtāni at 2.28). The verse contrasts two disciplines: one offers the senses themselves into 'the fires of restraint' (withdrawal from sense-activity), the other offers the sense-objects into 'the fires of the senses' themselves (controlled engagement rather than withdrawal) — the same two postures already weighed against each other in ch. 3.6-7.
#27
L: All the-actions-of-the-senses, and the-actions-of-the-life-breaths, others, into-the-fire-of-the-discipline-of-self-restraint, kindled-by-knowledge, offer.
I: Others offer all the workings of the senses and of the vital breaths into the fire of the discipline of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
N: Prāṇa-karmāṇi, 'the actions of the vital breaths', extends verse 26's offering of the senses to prāṇa itself, the breath regulated by the practice taken up directly in the verses just after this batch (29-30). The fire receiving both offerings is now named outright as ātma-saṃyama-yoga, 'the discipline of self-restraint', and called jñāna-dīpite, 'kindled by knowledge' — tying this whole catalogue back to the jñānāgni, 'fire of knowledge', of verse 19.
#28
L: Sacrificers-by-substance, sacrificers-by-austerity, sacrificers-by-yoga, likewise, others; sacrificers-by-study-and-knowledge, and — ascetics, of-rigorous-vows.
I: Some sacrifice with material offerings, some through austerity, some through the discipline of yoga, and others still through study and the pursuit of knowledge — all of them ascetics bound by rigorous vows.
N: A list of yajña compounds, each a distinct karmadhāraya naming sacrifice by its means — dravya (material substance), tapas (austerity), yoga, and svādhyāya-jñāna (recitation and knowledge) — continuing the catalogue begun at verse 25 and carried on with the breath-offerings of verses 29-30 (the next batch). Yatayaḥ saṃśita-vratāḥ, 'ascetics of sharpened vows', names all these practitioners together as of one kind, however different their chosen means.
#29
L: Into-apāna they-offer prāṇa, into-prāṇa apāna — likewise others; the-two-courses-of-prāṇa-and-apāna having-restrained, intent-on-breath-restraint.
I: Some offer the outward breath into the downward breath, and others, in the same way, offer the downward breath into the outward; others still block the passage of both breaths and give themselves wholly to breath-restraint.
N: Continuing the catalog of sacrifices opened at verse 24 (each kind of austerity and study already named there and at verse 28 counted as a yajña), this verse turns specifically to breath-control as an inner sacrifice: prāṇa and apāna are two of the five vital breaths (prāṇa the outward/upward breath, apāna the downward), and offering one into the other names two complementary breathing exercises, exhalation and inhalation each treated as an oblation. Prāṇāyāma-parāyaṇāḥ, 'devoted to breath-restraint', names a further group who instead block both breaths' movement outright.
#30
L: Others, of-regulated-diet, the-breaths into-the-breaths offer; all these, indeed, [are] knowers-of-sacrifice, whose-sins-are-destroyed-by-sacrifice.
I: Others, restricting their food, offer their very breaths into their breaths; all of these are knowers of sacrifice, their sins consumed by it.
N: This closes the catalog of many forms of sacrifice begun at verse 24: niyatāhārāḥ, 'of restricted diet', names a further ascetic discipline alongside verse 29's breath-exercises, and prāṇān prāṇeṣu juhvati, 'offer the breaths into the breaths', restates that same practice without singling out prāṇa and apāna. Yajña-vidaḥ, 'knowers of sacrifice', and yajña-kṣapita-kalmaṣāḥ, 'whose sins are worn away by sacrifice' (echoing 3.13's yajña-śiṣṭāśinaḥ ... mucyante sarva-kilbiṣaiḥ), sum up the whole list: whatever its form, sacrifice performed with understanding purifies.
#31
L: Eaters-of-the-nectar-remnant-of-sacrifice go to-brahman, eternal; not this world there-is for-the-non-sacrificer — whence another, O best-of-the-Kurus?
I: Those who eat the nectar left over from sacrifice reach the eternal brahman; but for one who offers no sacrifice at all, even this world is not truly his, let alone the world beyond — best of the Kurus.
N: This concludes the whole sacrifice-teaching begun at verse 9 with its reward, and by contrast its absence: yajña-śiṣṭa-amṛta-bhujaḥ, 'eaters of the nectar-remnant of sacrifice' (echoing 3.13's yajña-śiṣṭāśinaḥ, now with amṛta, 'nectar, the deathless', added), reach brahma sanātanam, 'eternal brahman'. Ayajñasya, 'for one without sacrifice', is denied even nāyaṃ lokaḥ, 'this very world', so kuto 'nyaḥ, 'how much less another' — an argument from the lesser case to the greater. Kuru-sattama, 'best of the Kurus', is a new epithet of Arjuna in this chapter.
#32
L: Thus many-kinds-of sacrifices [are] spread-out in-the-mouth of-brahman; born-of-action know them all — thus having-known, you-shall-be-released.
I: Thus many kinds of sacrifice are laid out in the mouth of brahman; know that all of them are born of action, and knowing this, you shall be set free.
N: A summary of the whole catalog just given (verses 24-30): brahmaṇo mukhe, 'in the mouth of brahman', most likely continues the sense of brahman as the Veda already used at 3.15 (Śaṅkara reads it as 'proclaimed by the Veda'), rather than the cosmic absolute. Karma-jān, 'born of action', reduces every form just listed to a single source, closing the ring back to 3.15's own chain (karma to brahman to the imperishable) and preparing the sharper ranking of action against knowledge that follows.
#33
L: Better than-the-sacrifice-consisting-of-substance [is] the-sacrifice-of-knowledge, O scorcher-of-the-foe; all action, entire, O son-of-Pṛthā, in-knowledge culminates.
I: The sacrifice of knowledge is better than any sacrifice made of material things, scorcher of the foe; all action without exception, Pārtha, comes to its consummation in knowledge.
N: This turns the whole sacrifice-teaching (verses 9-32) toward its point: material sacrifice (dravya-mayāt yajñāt), however valuable, ranks below jñāna-yajñaḥ, 'the sacrifice consisting in knowledge' — the first explicit ranking of the two paths named back at 3.3. Parisamāpyate, 'is wholly concluded, culminates', answers verse 32's karma-jān: knowledge is what all action, whatever its outward form, ultimately serves and ends in. This opens the chapter's closing movement praising jñāna directly, which runs through verse 42.
#34
L: That know! by-prostration, by-questioning, by-service; they-will-teach to-you knowledge, the-knowers, the-seers-of-truth.
I: Learn that through humble submission, through questioning, and through service; those who know, who see the truth, will teach you that knowledge.
N: Tat viddhi, 'know that' (the jñāna just praised in verse 33), is answered at once by how: praṇipātena, 'by prostration', paripraśnena, 'by close questioning', and sevayā, 'by attendance, service' — the classical threefold approach to a teacher. Jñāninas tattva-darśinaḥ, 'the knowers, the seers of truth', names the qualified teacher directly, as distinct from mere book-learning.
#35
L: Which having-known, not again to-delusion thus you-shall-go, O Pāṇḍava; by-which beings, without-remainder, you-shall-see in-the-self and-then in-me.
I: Once you know it, you will never again fall into this kind of delusion, Pāṇḍava; by it you will see all beings, without exception, in the self, and then in me.
N: Yat jñātvā, 'having known which', points back to the knowledge just promised in verse 34, and states its effect in two stages: first negatively, na punar moham yāsyasi, 'you will not go again to delusion' (moha, the very confusion that opened Arjuna's dialogue at 2.1); then positively, seeing bhūtāny aśeṣeṇa ātmani, 'all beings without exception in the self', atho mayi, 'and then in me' — Kṛṣṇa's own person identified with the impersonal self, a move the poem develops fully from chapter 7 on.
#36
L: Even if you-are, of-sinners, of-all, the-worst-doer-of-sin — all evil, by-the-boat-of-knowledge alone, you-shall-cross-over.
I: Even if you are the worst sinner of all sinners, you will cross over all that evil by the raft of knowledge alone.
N: A rhetorical extreme (api cet, 'even if') pushes the claim of verses 33-35 to its limit: pāpa-kṛt-tamaḥ, 'the worst doer of sin', built on kṛt, '-doer' (the same agent-suffix as in karma-kṛt), is promised the same crossing (santariṣyasi, from tṝ, 'to cross') by jñāna-plavena, 'the raft of knowledge' — one memorable image for the chapter's whole argument that knowledge, not ritual purity, saves.
#37
L: Just-as fuel a-kindled fire reduces-to-ashes, O Arjuna, the-fire-of-knowledge all-actions reduces-to-ashes, so.
I: Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
N: The chapter's most vivid simile: samiddho 'gnir edhāṃsi bhasmasāt kurute, 'a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes', is matched term for term by jñānāgniḥ sarva-karmāṇi bhasmasāt kurute, 'the fire of knowledge reduces all action to ashes'. Bhasmasāt, 'into the state of ashes', is a fixed adverbial formation (noun + -sāt, 'into the condition of') repeated identically in both halves of the verse.
#38
L: Not, indeed, to-knowledge equal a-purifier, here, exists; that, by-itself, one-perfected-in-yoga, in-time, in-the-self finds.
I: Nothing here purifies as knowledge does; one who is perfected in yoga finds this of himself, in time, within the self.
N: Pavitram, 'a purifier' (the same word used of the Ganges, of ghee, of holy water), is claimed for jñāna without qualification: nothing here (iha) equals it. Sadṛśam here is a declined adjective agreeing with pavitram, not the fixed adverb of 3.33's sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate. Svayaṃ ... kālenātmani vindati, 'finds it by himself, in time, within the self', promises that the yoga-saṃsiddhaḥ, 'one perfected in yoga' (echoing 3.20's Janaka, who reached perfection through action alone), eventually arrives at this knowledge unaided — a ripening, not an extra achievement.
#39
L: The-faithful-one obtains knowledge, intent-on-that, whose-senses-are-controlled; knowledge having-obtained, supreme peace, without-delay, he-attains.
I: The man of faith obtains knowledge, devoted to it, his senses controlled; and having gained knowledge, he attains supreme peace without delay.
N: Śraddhāvān shows an old Vedic-style sandhi before labhate: its final -n nasalizes the following l rather than becoming plain -n or -ṃ, written with a candrabindu and a doubled ल (श्रद्धावाँल्लभते for śraddhāvān labhate). Tat-paraḥ, 'intent on that' (the knowledge itself), and saṃyata-indriyaḥ, 'senses restrained', name the two conditions — faith and discipline — for reaching jñāna, which then leads without delay (acireṇa) to parāṃ śāntim, 'supreme peace'.
#40
L: The-ignorant-one, and the-faithless-one, and the-one-whose-self-is-doubt, perishes; not this world there-is, not the-other, not happiness, for-the-one-whose-self-is-doubt.
I: But the ignorant, the faithless, the doubting soul is lost; for the man of doubting mind there is no this world, no world beyond, and no happiness.
N: The negative mirror of verse 39's promise: ajñaḥ, 'ignorant', aśraddadhānaḥ, 'without faith' (the opposite of śraddhāvān), and saṃśaya-ātmā, 'whose mind is doubt', are named together as one who vinaśyati, 'perishes' — the harshest verdict since 3.32's naṣṭān acetasaḥ. The triple na ... na ... na, neither this world nor the world beyond nor happiness, is the bleakest formula in the chapter.
#41
L: One-who-has-renounced-actions-by-yoga, one-whose-doubt-is-severed-by-knowledge, self-possessed — actions do-not bind, O Dhanaṃjaya.
I: Actions do not bind the man who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubt has been cut away by knowledge, and who is master of himself, Dhanaṃjaya.
N: A composite portrait gathers the chapter's two closing themes into one person: yoga-saṃnyasta-karmāṇam, 'having renounced action by yoga' (recalling 3.20's Janaka, who acted while inwardly free), and jñāna-saṃchinna-saṃśayam, 'whose doubt is severed by knowledge' (the very saṃśaya just diagnosed as fatal in verse 40), together with ātmavantam, 'self-possessed'. Na karmāṇi nibadhnanti, 'actions do not bind him', is the fullest answer yet to the anxiety about karma-bandhana first raised at verse 9. Dhanaṃjaya, 'winner of wealth', is a new epithet of Arjuna in this chapter.
#42
L: Therefore, arisen-from-ignorance, seated-in-the-heart, of-one's-own — by-the-sword-of-knowledge, having-cut this doubt, in-yoga take-your-stand — arise, O Bhārata!
I: So cut away, with the sword of knowledge, this doubt of yours that is born of ignorance and lodged in the heart; take your stand in yoga — arise, Bhārata!
N: The chapter's closing command gathers its own vocabulary one last time: ajñāna-sambhūtam, 'arisen from ignorance', names the saṃśayam, 'doubt', just diagnosed as deadly in verse 40, to be cut (chittvā, from chid, echoing verse 41's jñāna-saṃchinna-) by jñānāsinā, 'the sword of knowledge' — a weapon-image alongside verse 37's fire. Yogam ātiṣṭha uttiṣṭha, 'take your stand in yoga, arise', closes the chapter, and Kṛṣṇa's whole answer to Arjuna's opening question at verse 1, on a command to act rather than withdraw; the same verb ud-sthā, 'arise', recurs memorably at 2.3's kṣudraṃ hṛdayadaurbalyaṃ tyaktvottiṣṭha parantapa — a distinct occurrence, not to be confused with either that verse or with the poem's actual opening scene in chapter 1.
